archetype.name: Dual-Threat (pocket-first)
archetype.definition: A big-armed passer who wins from the pocket by attacking downfield, then uses his legs as a release valve on broken plays rather than as a designed-run engine.

report.headline: The 2025 version is back after three ugly weeks; the deep ball drives it.
report.take:
Maye's season is two stories. The first three weeks were a mess: a combined record of one win in three, turnovers in every game, and a -14.2 passing EPA day in Jacksonville. The last three look like the quarterback who finished third in EPA per play in 2025. Since Week 4 he is at 0.506 EPA per dropback, a 1.9% sack rate and a 1% interception rate, with 10 touchdowns against one pick, and New England is 3-0. That is not a hot streak layered on a mediocre player. It is a return to a level he sustained for 17 games last year, after a slow start.

The engine is downfield aggression. On throws of 20+ air yards he is at 0.758 EPA per attempt with a +15.5 CPOE. Everything thrown 10+ yards adds 35.1 EPA, while everything short of 10 adds only 6.8. The underneath game is close to neutral mostly because of the screens: 34 throws behind the line cost 14.1 EPA. He also holds the ball (3.1 seconds to throw) and pays for it less than he used to. His pressure-to-sack rate is 23.9%, down from 35.6% last year and 40.5% as a rookie. When the pocket breaks he takes off, and 20 scrambles at 0.874 EPA each with 12 first downs more than cover the sacks that extended plays produce. His bad-throw rate of 8.2% ranks fourth, the cleanest of his career.

The numbers hide two things. First, the schedule: the bad stretch came against Seattle, Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, defenses now ranked 2nd, 6th and 17th. The good stretch came against Buffalo (30th), Las Vegas (21st) and the Jets (11th). The rebound is real but flattered. Second, his completion percentage is 8.1 points below last year and his CPOE is 6 points lower. He is not the ultra-accurate 2025 passer yet. He is getting there by hunting bigger plays.

The recurring flaw is ball security when he presses. Seven interceptions rank 43rd of 45, five turnover-worthy fumbles sit underneath that, and three picks came in close fourth quarters. Some of that is the price of throwing deep, since he has three interceptions on 26 deep attempts. Some of it is a real habit carried from his rookie year. Going forward, the upside is real and the floor depends on how many of those throws he gives back.

strengths.title: Downfield throws carry the offense
strengths.body: His deep attempts are the most efficient part of his game by a wide margin, with accuracy well above expectation. This matches 2025, when his aDOT rose to 9.1 and he ranked third in EPA per play. That makes it a skill, not a fluke. Expect regression from the extreme deep rate, but this stays his best weapon.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for the hold
strengths.body: He extends plays and, when nothing opens, turns broken dropbacks into chunk gains and first downs. That is the payoff for a 3.1-second time to throw. His pressure-to-sack rate is the best of his career, so he is converting pressure into yardage rather than drive-killers. Repeatable as long as the line gives him a pocket to escape from.

strengths.title: Recent form at a top level
strengths.body: Over the last three games his efficiency per dropback, touchdown rate and sack avoidance are all far above his season marks. The interceptions have nearly stopped. His throw quality backs it up: the bad-throw rate ranks fourth in the league.

concerns.title: Turnovers remain the floor-lowering habit
concerns.body: His interception rate ranks near the bottom of qualifiers, with five turnover-worthy fumbles on top. Part of this is the cost of pushing the ball deep. Part of it is a career-long trait: he threw 10 picks as a rookie and ranked 42nd in interceptions in 2025. The recent clean stretch is encouraging, but it came against softer defenses.

concerns.title: Third down and the structured game
concerns.body: He is below zero in EPA on third down, converting under 40% with nearly seven yards to go on average. The scheme's under-center and screen work has been a drain. A running game ranked 26th in EPA leaves him in long-yardage spots and puts most of the burden on his arm.

concerns.title: Accuracy below his 2025 standard
concerns.body: His CPOE is 6 points lower than last year and his completion rate fell 8.1 points. He is less precise than the 2025 version, even if the deep ball hides it. Some of that is a tougher early schedule. Some of it is lower aggressiveness producing fewer layups. Watch whether it climbs back now that the offense is clicking.

trend.note: Negative passing EPA in each of the first three games gave way to +11, +29.5 and +12.6 in Weeks 4-6. Sacks and interceptions nearly vanished in that span, though the opponents also got easier.

nextGame.headline: A deep-ball passer meets the league's worst deep defense, short-handed up front
nextGame.body:
Chicago's pass defense is good overall (7th in EPA) and strangles short throws, ranking 3rd. But it ranks last in both deep EPA allowed and explosive pass rate. That lines up exactly with where Maye does his damage. The underneath game, already his weakest area, will be tough sledding. His day depends on whether he gets time to push the ball. The Bears get home pressure at the second-highest sack rate in the league. With the total at 50.5 and New England a 3-point road underdog, the Book expects points and a game where he has to throw.

Availability cuts both ways. Three Patriots linemen are questionable on a four-day turnaround: guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (89% of snaps), tackle Morgan Moses, seen in a walking boot, and center Ben Brown. A patched line against that pass rush is the real risk. Chicago's rush is thinner too. Montez Sweat is suspended and Dayo Odeyingbo is on IR, and linebacker T.J. Edwards (88% of snaps) is out, which softens the middle of the field. On the receiving side, Romeo Doubs is on IR and A.J. Brown was limited. That leaves more targets for DeMario Douglas, Hunter Henry and Mack Hollins, who have all been efficient.

keyMatchups.title: His deep ball vs. Chicago's soft shell
keyMatchups.body: Maye's best throws are vertical, and Chicago gives up more EPA on deep passes than any defense. The Bears' short-area stinginess should push him downfield anyway. Expect a few chunk shots to decide his line.

keyMatchups.title: Banged-up line vs. depleted rush
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's sack rate is the second-best in football, but two of its edge rushers are missing. New England may be without its starting guard, center and right tackle. Maye's ability to escape and scramble is the tiebreaker here.

keyMatchups.title: Secondary receivers vs. Bears' WR2 coverage
keyMatchups.body: Chicago has let second receivers score above their averages but has smothered third options. With Doubs out, whoever slides into that number-two role could feast. That could be A.J. Brown if he plays, or Mack Hollins.

nextGame.watch: Who starts at center, guard and right tackle for New England. If two or more of them sit, his deep shots and sack avoidance face a much bigger test.

restOfSeason.body:
The baseline is a quarterback closer to his 2025 form than to his September. The deep efficiency, scramble value and improved sack avoidance are rooted in skills he showed all of last year. The last-three-game rate of 0.506 EPA per dropback will cool, both because those defenses were soft and because deep-ball TD rates swing. Plan on something like 250-285 passing yards and around two touchdowns a game, with 25-35 rushing yards from scrambles.

Interceptions are the variable. His season rate projects to a lot of turnovers, his recent rate to very few, and the truth is probably in between at roughly 0.6-0.9 a game. Doubs' absence until after the Week 11 bye trims his depth of options. The health of the offensive line matters more than any single receiver, because his whole profile depends on holding the ball and pushing it downfield.
swingFactors: Offensive line health (Vera-Tucker, Moses, Ben Brown)
A.J. Brown's ankle and Doubs' post-bye return

confidence.note: Six games, with a sharp split driven partly by opponent quality; strong 2025 track record anchors it.
